title: Morton on clarinetists, Oliver and Keppard; last meeting
summary: Morton's opinions of clarinetists and trumpeters, Bechet, Mitchell and Oliver's memory; Russell's last sight of him outside the rhythm club.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Who were the great clarinetists? Favorites and rivals

blocks.x: I have a note here. He mentioned that there were

three great clarinetists in New Orleans. Piku, Lorenzo Tio, and George Bakke. He didn't think Big Eye Louie was really in the first class. Other people will tell you they think Big Eye was better than Piku and so on. So some of that could be a question of opinion. he thought Dodds wasn't really a first class clarinetist. He was all right. He was only on a couple of his records, maybe four sides or so. I don't know. I even asked him once, I said, is it true that Muggsy had recorded with him? And he said, yes. No, I don't know. As I say, I believe that 99% of the time Jelly told the truth. I mean, any of this spreading on about how good he was, I never thought he had to spread it on. You couldn't exaggerate it, but it's possible in certain little cases, certain things, he might have said yes, you know, just quiet me down, too. If I said his Muggsy on, he thought, because it's possible, it might have been that Natty Dominic thing, though, too, or something, he had a tone similar to muted style at times. So I don't know whether that's really true that all these people recorded with him or not, because he had no reason especially to brag that they did record with him. He talked, I asked him about the Oliver record, that autograph, and he seemed quite excited about Oliver, and about the solo, you might call it. He said, my God, what a memory that man had. He said, I would play a piano chorus or something like King Porter or Tom Cat just once, and Oliver would take it and remember every note that he played. He said, you can't find a man like that today. So he had a lot of respect for Oliver, but Kepford was his favorite trumpet player, and he seemed to think that Bolden was plenty good too, although he liked Kepford better. Had a more jazzy style evidently. But I'll go over these notes sometime and copy everything here that's fit to copy. Some funny little stories, little remarks about Sidney Bechet. He thought he was great too. He seemed to like George Mitchell. I always wondered why he used somebody who wasn't from New Orleans when he could have had a pick of people you think like Kepford or Louie or other people around Chicago when he made those records. But he talked quite a bit, thought he'd learn a lot from Kepford and Oliver. Actually, Mitchell did, in his interview that we have of his claims, he learned a lot from Oliver. He tried to play like Joe. He said, I never could make it though. Couldn't quite make it like those New Orleans fathers. I tried my best to play like Joe but I didn't really succeed. But the jelly said, Mitchell's a greater carnettist than Louis Armstrong. But of course he'd say that about a dozen other people. Evidently, he didn't like Louis too well. They wrote one tune together, the Wild Man Blues. I wish I'd questioned him about that to see what part they wrote, how they wrote it together and all. I didn't get so many things we could have asked him. And the last time I saw jelly was up after I'd been to California a year or so. He came back and a friend of mine took me up to jelly. He'd been seeing him every week about it, Herman Rosenberg, a fabulous guy around New York, which is a whole story anyway. He's been written up in the papers. He's dead now. We went up to see Sidney Bechet who'd just gotten back from Chicago. They'd had a session for Victor in memory of Johnny Dodds. He made this date, Blues for You, Johnny, which is really a pretty sick sounding tune, I thought. One of the very worst records ever made. They took some popular singer along and sang it all the way through. I know Sidney gave me the supposedly original manuscript. I don't know where that is. I'll have to find it someday and we'll copyright it. I doubt if it's in Sidney's handwriting, though. Somebody else must have written it out for him. But he also played some opera stuff like the aria from Pagliacci, you know, the one that Caruso and all of them sing where you start out laughing and practically cry and all that stuff. And Sidney was wonderful. I mean, he's a dramatic player. He could play all that opera stuff and really make it sound. Then we went down to the rhythm club. I guess that's what it was called, a big place where all the musicians would meet a big pool hall, mostly, and back. Jelly was back there playing pool and we waited outside there, not that we were, it was segregated or anything, but somehow we just waited outside. About five or ten minutes after he finished his game, he came out and began talking. I was so dumb, and I still am, but he invited me to come the next Monday to a rehearsal where they were rehearsing a new band and all. Henry Allen, I think Paul Barberin was in for a while, and he was always trying to get a new band together. Somehow I never got to that rehearsal and a month later, Jelly left town, and a month later I left town, never did see him again.
